newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Fidel Ramos aims to push APEC into high gear.
newsitem.headline: Fidel Ramos aims to push APEC into high gear.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos, credited with taking the Philippines by the scruff of the neck and masterminding its economic rebirth, now has his sights set on concrete action from the APEC summit here in November.

Ramos told Reuters in an interview late on Wednesday that the three previous APEC (Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation) summits had laid the groundwork for what is potentially the world's biggest, richest and most diverse economic grouping.
"But now the action must start," he said.

Ramos, a West Point graduate and former career soldier whose work habits leave his staff exhausted, will serve as chairman for an APEC summit that U.S. President Bill Clinton and 15 other Asia-Pacific leaders are to attend in November.

The first summit in Seattle was about "visioning", while the second in Bogor, Indonesia, produced the timetable for APEC to liberalise trade and investment throughout the region by 2010 for developed members and 2020 for less advanced economies, Ramos said.
The third, in Osaka, yielded an action plan.

"This is now going to be the fourth summit of economic leaders and the chair, the Philippines, is expected to move the APEC process much faster and further forwards compared to the three other summits," Ramos said.
The president said hosting APEC was a great challenge for the Philippines.
"It's a greater challenge for me to be the chairman of the economic leaders' summit. We therefore are preparing as hard as we can...(for) the substantive agenda that we must tackle," he said.

Ramos took office in 1992 when the Philippine economy was in shambles, with power cuts lasting up to 10 hours a day even in its main business districts and zero growth after years of political turmoil and natural disasters.

This year's summit, on November 25 at Subic Bay just north of Manila, will be held against a backdrop of domestic political stability, strong growth that economists believe is sustainable and a resurgence of foreign investment.
Ramos was confident the Philippines could achieve its goal of pushing APEC towards action rather than words.

"We'll give it our best try. As we've overcome various challenges in the past I'm very confident that we can do in the Philippines in 1996 what we set out to do as the new APEC hosts. I'm sure we can do it," he said.
The Philippines plans to give the Subic summit and the ministerial meeting that precedes it a distinctive twist by providing the private sector a much higher profile than at previous APEC meetings.

"We have suggested an APEC business forum be included in these 1996 meetings so that we can really get the leaders of the private business sector all over APEC to interact more effectively and productively," Ramos said.

APEC members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Taiwan, Thailand, Singapore, and the United States.
